1. **Idea:** The animation compares two illustrative homeowners, Leo and Tessa. Each has a house and a stack of gold coins. Each also has a horizontal bar showing their own loan's interest rate. The on-screen text says the stack shows "how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit," and the source is labeled as the Freddie Mac weekly mortgage survey. So it appears to be about the gap between 15-year and 30-year mortgage rates, and what that gap means for each person's choice between putting money into the house or holding it elsewhere.

2. **What changes:** Mostly the text. Frame 1 has only the title. Frame 2 adds "your bar = your loan's own rate." Frame 3 adds "your stack = how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit." Frame 6 adds "a dollar in the house is hard to get back." The pictures change very little. In frame 1 a small pointer or arrow appears near Tessa's figure. Tessa's coin stack is taller than Leo's. The bars and the dashed empty box on the right stay roughly the same.

3. **Meaning:** The rate on your own loan is what matters when you weigh extra mortgage payments against investing. How far apart the 15-year and 30-year rates are is a separate piece of information. Money put into a house is illiquid, because it is "hard to get back." The "US only · history, not a forecast" and "ILLUSTRATIVE" labels say the figures are examples and not predictions.

4. **Advice:** There is no explicit instruction. A viewer might take away a loose guideline: compare your own loan's rate to what you could expect to earn elsewhere, and remember that extra money paid into the house is hard to recover. The frames don't say which option to choose, and they don't show an investment return to compare against.

5. **Source of the takeaway:** The comparison guideline in 4 is my own inference. The animation's text only supports the pieces: your own rate, the 15-year/30-year gap, and that money in the house is hard to get back. It never tells the viewer to pay extra or to invest, and it gives no numbers for either option.

For your situation, with a roughly $320,000 mortgage and a 15-year payment you can just afford, this image doesn't answer whether to pay extra or invest. It does point to two things to check. One is your own loan's rate. The other is how much liquidity you would give up by sending extra cash into the house.
